title: AI Might Not Be Coming for Lawyers' Jobs Anytime Soon
author: Grace Huckins

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious account: AI is already reshaping routine associate work and pressuring billable-hour economics and apprenticeship, but current reasoning limitations, liability, regulation and the need for human accountability constrain near-term substitution. It reinforces the need for redesigned training rather than claiming imminent lawyer replacement.
qs: While AI is reshaping the grunt work of the profession, the end of lawyers may not be arriving anytime soon.
Still, as AI takes on some associate work, law firms may need to reinvent their training system.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central concern that automating junior work can remove the repetitive experience through which associates develop expertise, and it endorses more formal training to replace lost apprenticeship opportunities. Its evidence is practitioner testimony and a training recommendation rather than proof of profession-wide displacement or of any specific replacement model’s effectiveness.
qs: “When junior work dries up, you have to have a more formal way of teaching than hoping that an apprenticeship works,” says Ethan Mollick, a management professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.

“I’m worried that I’m not getting the same reps that senior attorneys got,” he says, referring to the repetitive training that has long defined the early experiences of lawyers.** **“On the other hand, it is very nice to have a semi–knowledge expert to just ask questions to that’s not a partner who’s also very busy.”   Even though an AI job apocalypse looks distant, the uncertainty sticks with him.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure

It argues that exam and professional-benchmark scores omit important features of practice, reports reliability gaps despite substantial criterion-level scores, and acknowledges routine uses while rejecting near-term substitution. It does not directly establish the cluster’s strict complete-task/all-pass findings.

kp.k: Automation forecasts have not established imminent lawyer replacement
kp.d: Huckins contrasts early displacement expectations with continuing technical and institutional constraints. The article reports researchers' March 2023 claim that GPT-4 excelled on the Uniform Bar Exam and an industry report's prediction that 44% of legal work could be automated. It also reports that Clifford Chance cut 10% of its London staff last month, citing increased AI use as a reason, without treating this incident as evidence of profession-wide displacement.
qs: But for all the hype, LLMs are still far from thinking like lawyers—let alone replacing them.
While AI is reshaping the grunt work of the profession, the end of lawyers may not be arriving anytime soon.

kp.k: Firms are experimenting extensively with AI-assisted routine work
kp.d: The article describes adoption of ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Harvey and CoCounsel, alongside internally developed tools built on frontier models. Firms are offering AI boot camps and allowing associates to bill hundreds of hours for experimentation. It reports the American Bar Association's 2024 finding that 47.8% of attorneys at firms employing 500 or more lawyers used AI. Applications include document review, contract drafting and initial research.
qs: Law firms are experimenting with general-purpose tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot and specialized legal tools like Harvey and Thomson Reuters’ CoCounsel, with some building their own in-house tools on top of frontier models.
The legal tech industry entered a boom as law firms began adopting generative AI to mine mountains of documents and draft contracts, work ordinarily done by junior associates.

kp.k: Litigators report limits on novel reasoning and argument development
kp.d: Junior associate Lucas Hale uses Relativity for long documents and Copilot for drafting citations but reports hallucinations, digressions and failures on complex ChatGPT queries. Senior associate Allison Douglis uses an LLM to begin research but says it struggles with ambiguous law and developing litigation arguments. These are practitioners' reported experiences and judgments, not measured performance findings.
qs: “In the case where we have a very narrow question or a question of first impression for the court,” he says, referring to a novel legal question that a court has never decided before, “that’s the kind of thinking that the tool can’t do.”
“When it comes to actually fleshing out and developing an argument as a litigator, I don’t think they’re there,” she says.
“Right now, I would much rather work with a junior associate than an AI tool,” she says.

kp.k: Bar exam success does not establish practice readiness
kp.d: Huckins argues that standardized legal examinations test memorization and application to hypothetical situations rather than strategic judgment in complex circumstances or argument construction in unsettled law. The article also cautions that training models to perform well on benchmarks need not improve their reasoning.
qs: But passing a standardized test isn’t the same as practicing law.

The exam tests whether people can memorize legal rules and apply them to hypothetical situations—not whether they can exercise strategic judgment in complicated realities or craft arguments in uncharted legal territory.

kp.k: Professional Reasoning Benchmark identifies substantial reliability gaps
kp.d: ScaleAI's Professional Reasoning Benchmark, published in November, evaluated leading LLMs on legal and financial tasks designed by professionals. The article reports that the best model scored only 37% on the most difficult legal problems, representing a share of evaluation points rather than a percentage of cases answered correctly. Models made inaccurate judgments and sometimes reached correct conclusions through incomplete or opaque reasoning. Lead author Afra Feyza Akyurek interprets the results as showing that tools cannot substitute for lawyers.
qs: The study found that the models have critical gaps in their reliability for professional adoption, with the best-performing model scoring only 37% on the most difficult legal problems, meaning it met just over a third of possible points on the evaluation criteria.
The models frequently made inaccurate legal judgments, and if they did reach correct conclusions, they did so through incomplete or opaque reasoning processes.
“The tools actually are not there to basically substitute [for] your lawyer,” says Afra Feyza Akyurek, the lead author of the paper.

kp.k: Mercor results highlight costly-error constraints on economic usefulness
kp.d: Mercor's AI Productivity Index, published in September and updated in December, found substantial limitations in legal work. Its best-performing model scored 77.9% on legal tasks, satisfying roughly four out of five evaluation criteria. The article attributes to the study's early version the qualification that performance potentially valuable in some industries might be unusable where errors are costly.
qs: The best-performing model scored 77.9% on legal tasks, meaning it satisfied roughly four out of five evaluation criteria.
A model with such a score might generate substantial economic value in some industries, but in fields where errors are costly, it may not be useful at all, the early version of the study noted.

kp.k: Legal ambiguity and fragmented records complicate model learning
kp.d: Law professor Jon Choi cautions that even newer professional benchmarks fail to capture the most subjective and difficult real-world legal questions. He identifies ambiguity, questions without a single right answer, unrecorded legal work and lengthy documents distributed across hierarchically related legal authorities as obstacles to training models for legal reasoning.
qs: “These questions, although more challenging than those in past benchmarks, still don’t fully reflect the kinds of subjective, extremely challenging questions lawyers tackle in real life,” says Jon Choi
Making matters worse, a lot of legal work isn’t recorded in ways that can be used to train the models, he says.
When it is, documents can span hundreds of pages, scattered across statutes, regulations, and court cases that exist in a complex hierarchy.

kp.k: Humanlike reasoning limitations remain a proposed explanation
kp.d: Stanford law professor Julian Nyarko suggests that models may lack the ability to simulate scenarios and predict outcomes, potentially limiting complex legal reasoning. The article presents this as a possible fundamental limitation of current next-word-prediction training, not an established finding.
qs: But a more fundamental limitation might be that LLMs are simply not trained to think like lawyers.
“The reasoning models still don’t fully reason about problems like we humans do,” says Julian Nyarko, a law professor at Stanford Law School.

kp.k: Graduate employment data counter immediate displacement expectations
kp.d: The article reports National Association for Law Placement data showing that 93.4% of 2024 law school graduates were employed within 10 months, the highest recorded rate, and that graduates working in law firms increased by 13% from 2023 to 2024. It contrasts these figures with early signs of AI effects on entry-level workers more broadly. Ropes & Gray's chief of attorney talent, Amy Ross, separately says the firm is not currently reducing headcount.
qs: The number of graduates working in law firms rose by 13% from 2023 to 2024.
“We’re not reducing headcounts at this point,” said Amy Ross, the chief of attorney talent at the law firm Ropes & Gray.

kp.k: Low risk tolerance may limit labor-market disruption
kp.d: MIT economist Mert Demirer predicts some legal labor-market impact but not a major one. He expects AI to be useful for information discovery and summarization, while arguing that current capabilities and law's low tolerance for error make complex work less automatable. Future capability improvements remain uncertain.
qs: “I will expect some impact on the legal profession’s labor market, but not major,” says Mert Demirer, an economist at MIT.
“AI is going to be very useful in terms of information discovery and summary,” he says
Capabilities may evolve over time, but that’s a big unknown.

kp.k: Billing incentives, liability and regulation constrain substitution
kp.d: Beyond model capabilities, Huckins identifies institutional barriers: productivity gains reduce billable hours and challenge firms' dominant business model; liability and clients' potential preference for human accountability discourage replacement; and regulation could constrain deployment. These are proposed mechanisms rather than quantified effects or analysis of specific professional rules.
qs: It’s not just that the models themselves are not ready to replace junior lawyers.
Liability looms large for lawyers, and clients may still want a human on the hook.
Regulations could also constrain how lawyers use the technology.

kp.k: Automated junior tasks threaten apprenticeship-based professional formation
kp.d: Wharton professor Ethan Mollick recommends more formal teaching if AI reduces junior work. Junior associate Zach Couger reports using ChatGPT to review contracts previously examined manually and worries about losing the repetitive practice senior lawyers received. He also values AI as an accessible source of answers when partners are busy. His fear of belonging to the last class of large-firm associates is personal uncertainty, not a demonstrated employment trend.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Huckins argues that AI is changing routine legal work but is not yet positioned to replace lawyers broadly; interviewed practitioners and researchers identify capability, institutional and training constraints.
pts.d: Huckins describes adoption for document review and contract drafting, tasks ordinarily performed by junior associates, while arguing that hallucinations, ambiguous law, novel questions and synthesis across legal authorities limit substitution. Lucas Hale reports using AI for routine tasks but says little of his current litigation work can be outsourced to it. Allison Douglis uses an LLM to begin research but prefers junior associates for developing litigation arguments. Afra Feyza Akyurek says current tools cannot substitute for a lawyer. Jon Choi argues that even newer professional benchmarks do not fully capture difficult, subjective legal questions, and identifies ambiguity, unrecorded work and dispersed legal materials as obstacles to learning legal reasoning. Julian Nyarko suggests that models may lack the mental model of the world needed for complex legal reasoning; Huckins presents a possible ceiling on next-word-prediction models as a possibility rather than an established finding. Mert Demirer predicts some, but not major, legal labor-market effects: discovery and summarization should benefit, while complex tasks remain less automatable. Huckins also identifies hourly billing incentives, liability, client preferences for human accountability and possible regulatory constraints as barriers to displacement. Ethan Mollick predicts a need for more formal training if AI removes junior work. Zach Couger reports substantially easier contract review but worries about losing repetitive learning opportunities. The article contrasts these qualified claims with an earlier industry prediction that 44% of legal work could be automated and a reported Clifford Chance staff reduction citing AI as one reason.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article combines professional benchmarks, adoption and employment statistics, a reported staffing reduction, practitioner experiences and expert judgments; these supply different kinds of support rather than a single measured displacement estimate.
pts.d: Huckins cites ScaleAI’s Professional Reasoning Benchmark, published in November, in which the best-performing model earned 37% of possible evaluation points on the most difficult legal problems; models also produced inaccurate judgments or incomplete or opaque reasoning. Mercor’s AI Productivity Index, published in September and updated in December, reported a best legal-task score of 77.9% of evaluation criteria. Neither figure is presented as a percentage of jobs automated or a measured hallucination rate. The early Mercor study cautioned that performance capable of generating value elsewhere might not be useful where errors are costly. The article contrasts these professional evaluations with GPT-4’s reported March 2023 Uniform Bar Exam performance and a contemporaneous industry automation prediction. ABA figures indicate AI use by 47.8% of attorneys at firms with at least 500 lawyers in 2024. NALP figures show 93.4% employment within 10 months for 2024 law graduates and a 13% rise in graduates working in law firms from 2023 to 2024; Huckins uses these to support the claim that labor statistics have not yet shown lawyer displacement. Amy Ross says Ropes & Gray is not reducing headcount. As a contrasting case, Huckins reports that Clifford Chance cut 10% of its London staff in the preceding month, citing increased AI use as a reason, without establishing that all affected staff were lawyers or that AI was the sole cause. Hale’s and Douglis’s accounts of unreliable outputs and Couger’s contract-review experience are practitioner testimony. Choi’s and Nyarko’s explanations of reasoning limits, Demirer’s labor-market forecast and Mollick’s training warning are attributed expert judgments rather than measured future outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The central prediction is near-term and conditional on current capabilities, costly errors and institutional constraints; the article does not predict permanent immunity from displacement.
pts.d: The article’s frame is 2025, with historical reference points including the 2022 generative-AI boom, March 2023 bar-exam and automation claims, and 2024 adoption and graduate-employment data. The professional benchmarks are described as published in November and in September with a December update; the Clifford Chance reduction is described relatively as occurring 'Last month.' Practitioners restrict their assessments to current tools and their own work. Douglis explicitly allows that extraordinarily rapid improvement could change her preference for a junior associate. Demirer conditions limited automation of complex tasks on present capabilities and law’s low tolerance for risk, and treats future capability development as unknown. Nyarko’s proposed reasoning limitation is speculative. Institutional constraints are presented as factors that may shape adoption, not proof that replacement is impossible. Mollick’s training prediction is conditional on junior work drying up. Couger’s fear of belonging to the last class of big-firm associates is reported as personal uncertainty, not an established labor-market forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The article focuses on law firms, particularly junior associates and litigators, while identifying consequences for senior lawyers, firm management and clients.
pts.d: Junior associates face automation of document-heavy tasks, possible reductions in repetitive on-the-job learning and uncertainty about future hiring, alongside immediate convenience and assistance. Litigators are portrayed by Hale and Douglis as less substitutable where their work requires novel legal reasoning, strategic judgment and argument development. Senior associates and partners remain important sources of expertise and supervision; Douglis still prefers junior human assistance, while Couger values asking AI questions without taking a busy partner’s time. Large firms are experimenting with tools and training, but greater productivity may reduce billable hours and challenge their dominant business model. Firm leaders may need to redesign associate education even without cutting headcount. The reported Clifford Chance reduction concerns London staff, whereas Ropes & Gray’s reported position is that it is not reducing headcounts. Clients are affected by reliability, costly mistakes, liability and the preference for a human accountable for legal work. Graduate-employment statistics concern recent law-school cohorts, not every legal occupation. The source does not offer a concrete prediction about access to justice or alternative legal service providers.
